pages.title: Our Lady of Lourdes
pages.address: Sanctuaire Notre-Dame de Lourdes, 1 avenue Monseigneur Théas, 65108 Lourdes, France
pages.admission: Free entry to the Sanctuary, Grotto, basilicas and baths. No reservation is needed to pray.
pages.accessibility_summary: Ramps, lifts and level paths across the Sanctuary, with free wheelchair loans. The Way of the Cross on the hill is steep, with steps.
pages.worship_note: Mass every day in several languages. In season, the Rosary at the Grotto, the Eucharistic procession and the torchlight procession at night.
pages.account_tradition: Between February 11 and July 16, 1858, Bernadette Soubirous said a lady dressed in white appeared to her 18 times at the Grotto of Massabielle. The Lady asked for prayer and penance for sinners, led Bernadette to a spring, and asked for a chapel and for people to come in procession. On March 25 she gave her name: "I am the Immaculate Conception."
pages.account_church_judgment: Bishop Bertrand-Sévère Laurence of Tarbes opened a commission of inquiry in July 1858, and it studied the events for nearly four years. In a pastoral letter dated January 18, 1862, he judged that the Immaculate Mary, Mother of God, really appeared to Bernadette, and that the faithful are justified in believing it. The same letter recognized seven healings as miraculous. Pope Pius XI canonized Bernadette on December 8, 1933.
pages.account_findings: A person who believes they were healed reports it to the Lourdes Medical Bureau, founded in 1883, where doctors document the case. Cases that stay unexplained go to the International Medical Committee of Lourdes. If the committee finds no medical explanation, the bishop of the person's home diocese decides whether to declare a miracle. As of August 2026, the Sanctuary counts 72 recognized miracles among about 7,500 recorded healings.
pages.account_teaching: Church approval means the Lourdes apparitions are worthy of belief and devotion there is encouraged. Approved private revelations are not part of the deposit of faith, so no Catholic is required to believe them (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 67).
pages.prep_prayer:
Our Lady of Lourdes, pray for us. Saint Bernadette, pray for us.

Bernadette was praying the Rosary when Our Lady first appeared. Many pilgrims pray it at the Grotto, along with the names of the sick they have promised to remember.
pages.prep_readings:
• Luke 1:26–38, the Annunciation: Mary is greeted as "full of grace," which connects to the name she gave at Lourdes.
  • John 2:1–11, the wedding at Cana: Mary brings people's needs to Jesus.
  • John 5:1–9, the pool of Bethesda: Jesus heals a sick man. A good reading before visiting the baths.
  • Ezekiel 47:1–12: water flows from the temple and brings life and healing, an echo of the spring Bernadette uncovered.
  • Isaiah 66:10–14: God comforts his people like a mother comforts her child.

pages.title: Our Lady of Medjugorje (Queen of Peace)
pages.address: St. James Parish Church, 88266 Međugorje, Bosnia and Herzegovina
pages.time_needed: 2–3 days to pray at St. James and climb both hills
pages.admission: Free. No tickets for the church, the grounds, the hills or the evening prayer program.
pages.accessibility_summary: The church, square and Risen Christ statue are on flat ground. Apparition Hill and Cross Mountain have steep, rocky paths.
pages.worship_note: Rosary and Mass every evening, with morning Masses in several languages. Evening times change with the season, so check the parish program.
pages.account_tradition: On June 24, 1981, young people from the parish said they saw the Virgin Mary on Podbrdo hill. By the next day the group was the six later called the visionaries: Ivanka Ivanković, Mirjana Dragičević, Vicka Ivanković, Ivan Dragičević, Marija Pavlović and Jakov Čolo. They said she called herself the Queen of Peace and asked people to pray, fast, go to Confession and Mass, and turn back to God. Some of them say they still receive messages today.
pages.account_church_judgment: On September 19, 2024, with Pope Francis's approval, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith granted a nihil obstat to the spiritual experience of Medjugorje. Catholics may take part in public devotion there. The Dicastery did not declare the apparitions supernatural, calls the messages "alleged," and says no one is obliged to believe them. In 2021 the Holy See appointed a special Apostolic Visitor for the parish, Archbishop Aldo Cavalli.
pages.account_findings: The Dicastery's note describes abundant conversions, a frequent return to the sacraments, especially the Eucharist and Confession, numerous confessions, and many vocations to the priesthood, religious life and marriage. It also mentions reconciliations between spouses and works of charity that grew up around the parish.
pages.account_teaching: Medjugorje is a matter of private devotion, not something Catholics are required to believe. The faithful may draw spiritual help from the messages as edifying texts without treating any of them as proven to come from Our Lady.
pages.prep_prayer:
Queen of Peace, pray for us.

This title of Our Lady is in the Litany of Loreto, where Pope Benedict XV added it in 1917. Many pilgrims pray the Rosary while climbing Apparition Hill.
pages.prep_readings:
• John 14:27: Jesus gives his peace, the heart of the title Queen of Peace.
  • Luke 1:46–55: Mary's Magnificat, a prayer of praise.
  • John 19:25–27: Jesus gives Mary to the disciple as his mother.
  • Luke 15:11–32: the Prodigal Son, for the many who go to Confession here.
  • Matthew 5:1–12: the Beatitudes, including "Blessed are the peacemakers."
pages.primary_references:
• Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith: note "The Queen of Peace" (Sept. 19, 2024)
  • Holy See Press Office: presentation of the note
  • Vatican News: Medjugorje and the Church, a history
  • Parish of St. James, Medjugorje

pages.title: Basilica of St. Francis of Assisi
pages.time_needed: About 2 hours for both churches and the tomb
pages.admission: Free, with no ticket. Groups and guided visits book ahead. Cover shoulders and knees; no photos inside.
pages.accessibility_summary: Each church has its own street-level entrance, but stairs link the two levels and the tomb. Ask the information office about lift access.
pages.worship_note: Mass every day in the Lower Church. The tomb also opens on Friday and Saturday evenings for quiet prayer. Check times before you go.
pages.account_tradition: St. Francis died in 1226 and was first buried in the church of San Giorgio in Assisi. In 1230 his body was moved into the new basilica and sealed deep beneath the high altar, out of sight of pilgrims, and over time the exact spot was forgotten. After earlier searches failed, workers found the stone tomb on the night of December 12, 1818.
pages.account_church_judgment: Pope Gregory IX declared Francis a saint on July 16, 1228 and laid the basilica's first stone the next day. In 1820 Pope Pius VII confirmed that the remains found in 1818 were those of St. Francis and had a crypt carved from the rock so pilgrims could pray at the tomb. The church is a papal basilica, cared for by the Franciscan friars of the Sacro Convento.
pages.account_findings: With Pope Paul VI's approval, the relics were examined again in 1978 and sealed in a clear case to protect them. A check in 2015 found no significant change. From February 22 to March 22, 2026, for the 800th anniversary of his death, the remains were shown to the public for the first time.
pages.account_teaching: Catholics do not worship saints or relics. They honor the saints as friends of God whose lives point to Christ and ask for their prayers, and the Church counts the veneration of relics among good forms of popular devotion (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1674).
pages.prep_prayer:
Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart. Give me right faith, sure hope and perfect charity. Fill me with understanding and knowledge, that I may fulfill your command. Amen.

The Prayer before the Crucifix, which Franciscan tradition holds St. Francis prayed before the San Damiano cross. English translations vary slightly.
pages.prep_readings:
• Galatians 6:14–17: Paul boasts only in the cross and bears the marks of Jesus, words that fit Francis and his stigmata.
  • Matthew 11:25–30: read on his feast day, October 4. God reveals himself to the little ones.
  • Matthew 10:7–10: Jesus sends the disciples out with no money or extra clothes, a call Francis took literally.
  • Matthew 19:21: "Go, sell what you have and give to the poor," a passage that shaped the first friars.
  • Psalm 148: all creation praises the Lord, an echo of Francis's Canticle of the Creatures.

pages.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe
pages.address: Fray Juan de Zumárraga 2, Villa Gustavo A. Madero, 07050 Ciudad de México, Mexico
pages.time_needed: 2–4 hours for the basilicas, chapels and Tepeyac hill
pages.admission: Free to enter the plaza, both basilicas and the chapels. The museum charges a fee.
pages.accessibility_summary: The plaza and the New Basilica are at ground level. The Capilla del Cerrito on Tepeyac hill is reached by stairs, with a ramp on the southeast side.
pages.worship_note: The New Basilica is open daily with Mass about once an hour. Expect very large crowds around December 12. Check the official schedule before you go.
pages.account_tradition: According to tradition, in December 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared several times on Tepeyac hill to Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin, an Indigenous convert, and asked that a church be built there. Bishop Juan de Zumárraga asked for a sign. On December 12, Juan Diego gathered roses on the hilltop, and when he opened his tilma before the bishop, her image was on the cloth.
pages.account_church_judgment: Guadalupe never received a modern-style verdict on the apparitions. The Church approved the devotion step by step: sworn testimony was gathered in 1665 and 1666, and on May 25, 1754, Pope Benedict XIV named Our Lady of Guadalupe patroness of New Spain and approved a proper Mass and Office for December 12. Leo XIII authorized the crowning of the image in 1895, and St. John Paul II canonized Juan Diego at the Basilica on July 31, 2002.
pages.account_findings: Studies of the tilma have reached different conclusions. In 1979 infrared photographs, researchers reported no underdrawing beneath the original image along with later painted additions, while others have argued the image was made by human hands. Claims of tiny figures in the eyes remain disputed. None of these claims is settled, and the Church does not rest its approval on them.
pages.account_teaching: Guadalupe is an approved private revelation. Such revelations add nothing to the faith, so Catholics may honor this devotion but are not required to believe it (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 67).
pages.prep_prayer:
Holy Mary of Guadalupe, Mother of the true God, pray for us.

"Am I not here, I who am your mother?" Our Lady's words to Juan Diego, as recorded in the Nican Mopohua.
pages.prep_readings:
• Revelation 12:1–6: the woman clothed with the sun, echoed in the rays and moon on the tilma.
  • Zechariah 2:14–17: "Sing and rejoice, O daughter Zion! I am coming to dwell among you," a reading for December 12.
  • Luke 1:39–47: Mary brings Christ to Elizabeth, as she came to the people of the Americas.
  • 1 Corinthians 1:26–29: God chooses the lowly, like Juan Diego, to carry his message.
  • Isaiah 66:13: "As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you."
pages.primary_references:

  • St. John Paul II, homily for the canonization of Juan Diego (2002)

pages.title: Our Lady of Fatima
pages.address: Santuário de Fátima, Rua de Santa Isabel 360, 2495-424 Fátima, Portugal
pages.time_needed: A full day for the Sanctuary, Aljustrel and the Valinhos
pages.admission: Free. The Sanctuary is open day and night, and the seers' houses in Aljustrel are free.
pages.accessibility_summary: Most of the Sanctuary is accessible, with space set aside at services for wheelchair users. Aljustrel and the Valinhos are about 2 km away.
pages.worship_note: Many Masses daily in Portuguese and other languages. The 9:30 pm Rosary at the Chapel of the Apparitions ends with a candlelight procession every night.
pages.account_tradition: In 1916 three shepherd children from Aljustrel, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, reported three visits from an angel. Between May 13 and October 13, 1917, they said a Lady appeared to them over a small holm oak at the Cova da Iria, most often on the 13th of the month; the August visit came on the 19th at the Valinhos. They said she urged prayer, especially the Rosary, and sacrifice for sinners, and called herself the Lady of the Rosary.
pages.account_church_judgment: After a canonical commission studied the events, Bishop José Alves Correia da Silva of Leiria issued a pastoral letter on October 13, 1930, declaring the children's visions worthy of belief and permitting devotion to Our Lady of the Rosary of Fátima. Pope Francis canonized Francisco and Jacinta at Fátima on May 13, 2017. Lúcia, who died in 2005, was declared Venerable in 2023.
pages.account_findings: The Shrine says about 70,000 people came on October 13, 1917, expecting a sign. Many said that after heavy rain the sun looked like a pale, spinning disc that gave off colored light and seemed to fall toward the earth, and that their soaked clothes dried quickly. Accounts varied: some saw only colors, and some saw nothing unusual.
pages.account_teaching: The Church treats Fátima as an approved private revelation. Such revelations add nothing to the faith (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 67); the Vatican's 2000 commentary calls private revelation "a help which is offered, but which one is not obliged to use."
pages.prep_prayer:
My God, I believe, I adore, I hope and I love You. I ask pardon of You for those who do not believe, do not adore, do not hope and do not love You.

The Pardon Prayer. In Sister Lúcia's account, the Angel of Peace taught it to the three children in 1916.
pages.prep_readings:
• Genesis 3:15: God's first promise of a woman whose offspring will defeat evil.
  • Luke 1:26–38: the Annunciation, the first joyful mystery of the Rosary.
  • John 19:25–27: at the cross Jesus gives Mary to us as our mother.
  • Mark 1:14–15: "Repent, and believe in the gospel," the call at the heart of Fátima.
  • Revelation 12:1: the woman clothed with the sun.

pages.title: Our Lady of Knock
pages.address: Knock Shrine, Knock, Claremorris, Co. Mayo, F12 Y226, Ireland
pages.time_needed: A half day for the chapels, Basilica and Museum
pages.admission: Free. The grounds, chapels, Basilica and Knock Museum have no entry charge, and parking is free.
pages.accessibility_summary: Free wheelchair loans, a free daily shuttle for people with limited mobility, wheelchair seating in each chapel, and accessible toilets.
pages.worship_note: Mass several times every day in the Parish Church and the Basilica, with daily Confession in the Chapel of Reconciliation. Times change with the season.
pages.account_tradition: On the rainy evening of August 21, 1879, fifteen people from Knock said they saw Our Lady, St. Joseph and St. John the Evangelist at the south gable wall of the parish church, beside an altar with a Lamb on it. No words were spoken. The witnesses stood in the rain and prayed the Rosary for about two hours.
pages.account_church_judgment: In October 1879 Archbishop John MacHale of Tuam set up a Commission of Enquiry, which found the witnesses' testimony "trustworthy and satisfactory." A second commission in 1935 and 1936 took sworn evidence from surviving witnesses and reached the same view. St. John Paul II made the church a basilica and visited in 1979, and in 2021 Pope Francis named Knock an International Shrine of Eucharistic and Marian Devotion.
pages.account_findings: Pilgrims reported cures from the first months after 1879, and crutches left at the gable became a familiar sight. In 2019, after review by the Knock Medical Bureau, Church leaders recognized the 1989 healing of a pilgrim, Marion Carroll, as having no medical explanation, the first officially recognized healing at Knock.
pages.account_teaching: Approved private revelations like Knock are not part of the deposit of faith, and Catholics are not required to believe them (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 67). They can help people live the Gospel more fully.
pages.prep_prayer:
Our Lady of Knock, Queen of Ireland, you gave hope to your people in a time of distress, and comforted them in sorrow. Our Lady of Knock, Health of the Sick, pray for us.

From the Prayer to Our Lady of Knock, Knock Shrine novena leaflet.
pages.prep_readings:
• Revelation 5:6–14: the Lamb standing at the throne, like the Lamb on the altar at Knock.
  • John 1:29–36: "Behold, the Lamb of God," pointing to the Eucharist at the center of the vision.
  • John 19:25–27: Mary and the beloved disciple John together at the Cross.
  • Matthew 1:18–25: St. Joseph, the faithful husband who stood beside Mary.
  • Revelation 12:1: the woman crowned in heaven, recalling Mary's crown in the vision.

pages.title: St. Peter's Basilica
pages.time_needed: 2–3 hours; add about 90 minutes each for the dome or the Scavi
pages.admission: Free entry. The dome, the Scavi tour of St. Peter's tomb and guided visits are booked on the official site.
pages.accessibility_summary: A reserved entrance for people with disabilities in the right side of the square, with a ramp to security. The Scavi and dome stairs aren't accessible.
pages.worship_note: Many Masses every day and Confession through most of the day. Adoration in the Blessed Sacrament Chapel, Monday to Saturday.
pages.account_tradition: Catholic tradition holds that St. Peter was martyred in Nero's circus on the Vatican Hill around AD 64 and buried in a cemetery nearby. Constantine built the first basilica over that grave in the 4th century. The present church, finished in 1626, stands on the same spot, with its high altar directly above the traditional tomb.
pages.account_church_judgment: In his Christmas message of 1950, Pope Pius XII announced that the tomb of the Apostle had been found, while noting that the bones could not be proven to be Peter's. On June 26, 1968, Pope Paul VI said that relics of Peter had been identified "in a manner considered convincing." Pope Francis displayed some of these relics publicly for the first time in November 2013.
pages.account_findings: Excavations from 1939 to 1949 uncovered a Roman cemetery under the basilica, a small 2nd-century shrine over a simple grave, and a nearby wall covered in early Christian graffiti. Most scholars accept the site as the place Christians honored as Peter's grave from very early on, but no one can prove scientifically whose bones were found.
pages.account_teaching: Jesus named Peter the rock on which he would build his Church, and the Church teaches that the Pope, Peter's successor as Bishop of Rome, is the lasting source and sign of unity among bishops and all the faithful (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 881–882).
pages.prep_prayer:
Let us pray for our Pope. May the Lord preserve him, give him life, and make him blessed upon the earth, and deliver him not up to the will of his enemies.

Traditional prayer for the Pope, based on Psalm 41.
pages.prep_readings:
• Matthew 16:13–19: Peter's confession and Jesus calling him the rock.
  • John 21:15–19: the risen Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep and foretells his death.
  • Luke 22:31–32: Jesus prays that Peter's faith will not fail.
  • 1 Peter 5:1–4: Peter, writing from Rome, urges leaders to shepherd God's flock.
  • 2 Peter 1:12–15: Peter speaks of his coming death and his care for the Church.
pages.primary_references:

  • St. Peter's Basilica: entering the basilica
  • St. Peter's Basilica: services for pilgrims (accessibility)

pages.title: Basilica of St. John Lateran
pages.address: Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano, 00184 Rome, Italy
pages.time_needed: 1.5–3 hours with the Scala Santa and Baptistery
pages.admission: The basilica and Baptistery are free. The cloister, museum, Sancta Sanctorum and excavations have separate tickets.
pages.accessibility_summary: Two ramps on the front forecourt, lifts in the portico, and another inside to the transept. The Scala Santa is climbed on the knees.
pages.worship_note: Several Masses every weekday in the side chapels, Sunday Masses at the papal altar, and weekday Eucharistic Adoration.
pages.account_tradition: Tradition holds that Emperor Constantine gave the Lateran property to the Bishop of Rome after the Church gained freedom in 313. Pope Sylvester I dedicated the basilica to Christ the Savior around 324, and it was later also dedicated to St. John the Baptist and St. John the Evangelist. It has been the Pope's cathedral as Bishop of Rome ever since.
pages.account_church_judgment: The Church honors the Lateran as "mother and head of all churches of the city and the world," words carved on its facade, and the whole Latin Church keeps the feast of its dedication every November 9. Each new pope formally takes possession of his cathedra here; Pope Leo XIV did so on May 25, 2025.
pages.account_findings: Excavations beneath the basilica found houses from the early Roman Empire, barracks of the emperor's mounted guard that Constantine disbanded, and the foundations of his first basilica. The finds match the historical record of Constantine building the church on imperial land.
pages.account_teaching: As the Pope's cathedral, the Lateran is a sign that every Catholic diocese is joined in faith and communion with the Bishop of Rome. Its feast also reminds us that we ourselves are God's living temple (1 Corinthians 3:16).
pages.prep_prayer:
O God, who from living and chosen stones prepare an eternal dwelling for your majesty, increase in your Church the spirit of grace you have bestowed, so that by new growth your faithful people may build up the heavenly Jerusalem.

Collect for the Feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, Roman Missal.
pages.prep_readings:
• Ezekiel 47:1–2, 8–9, 12: life-giving water flows from the Temple, read on the Lateran's feast.
  • 1 Corinthians 3:9–11, 16–17: you are God's building and temple.
  • John 2:13–22: Jesus cleanses the Temple and speaks of the temple of his body.
  • Psalm 46: God's presence makes the holy city glad.
  • John 19:13–17: Jesus before Pilate, recalled at the Scala Santa.

pages.title: Basilica of St. Mary Major
pages.address: Piazza di Santa Maria Maggiore, 00185 Rome, Italy
pages.time_needed: 1.5–2 hours; add an hour for the museum and Loggia
pages.admission: Free to enter the basilica. The museum, Loggia of Blessings and excavations need a ticket.
pages.accessibility_summary: A ramp at the main facade, ramps to the side chapels on request, accessible restrooms and a lift in the museum. The forecourt is cobbled.
pages.worship_note: Mass many times daily, mostly in the Pauline Chapel. Modest dress and a security check at the door. Pope Francis's tomb is in the left aisle.
pages.account_tradition: Tradition holds that in the 4th century, in the time of Pope Liberius, Mary asked for a church to be built where snow would fall, and snow covered the Esquiline Hill on August 5; white petals still fall during Mass each August 5. The basilica also keeps the Salus Populi Romani icon, which tradition credits to St. Luke, and the Holy Crib, wooden slats honored as part of the manger of Bethlehem.
pages.account_church_judgment: The present basilica dates to the 430s and is tied to the Council of Ephesus (431), which proclaimed Mary Theotokos, Mother of God; Pope Sixtus III's name stands on its triumphal arch. The Church keeps the Dedication of St. Mary Major on August 5 in its universal calendar, and Pius XII crowned the icon in 1954. Pope Francis was buried here in April 2025.
pages.account_findings: Historians note that the snow story was first written down centuries later, and excavations have not found remains of an earlier church from Liberius's time. The icon is very old, but its exact date is debated. The basilica reports that recent studies date the crib wood to the time of Christ, but details haven't been published.
pages.account_teaching: The Church calls Mary the Mother of God because the child she bore is truly God made man (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 495). This basilica, built to honor that truth, invites pilgrims to thank God for the Incarnation and to trust Mary as a mother.
pages.prep_prayer:
We fly to your protection, O holy Mother of God. Do not despise our petitions in our necessities, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin. Amen.

Sub tuum praesidium, one of the oldest known prayers to Mary.
pages.prep_readings:
• Luke 1:26–38: the Annunciation, the first scene on the triumphal arch.
  • Luke 2:1–20: Jesus laid in a manger, recalled by the Holy Crib.
  • Galatians 4:4–7: God's Son "born of a woman," the truth defended at Ephesus.
  • John 19:25–27: Jesus gives Mary to us as Mother.
  • Matthew 2:1–12: the Magi find the Child with Mary his mother.

pages.title: Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls
pages.admission: Free to enter the basilica. The cloister and archaeological area have a small ticket.
pages.accessibility_summary: The basilica publishes no details on ramps or step-free routes. Contact it before visiting or ask staff on arrival.
pages.worship_note: Mass several times daily, with more on Sundays. The Benedictine monks of the abbey pray here every day.
pages.account_tradition: Catholic tradition holds that St. Paul was beheaded outside Rome around AD 67, under Nero, at the place now called Tre Fontane. His body was buried in a cemetery beside the Via Ostiense, and his grave quickly became a place of pilgrimage. The basilica stands over that grave.
pages.account_church_judgment: Constantine built the first church over the tomb, and a much larger basilica was consecrated in 390. After the great fire of 1823 it was rebuilt on the same plan, and Pius IX dedicated it in 1854. Vatican archaeologists uncovered the sarcophagus beneath the altar between 2002 and 2006, and on June 28, 2009, Pope Benedict XVI announced the results of a probe inside it.
pages.account_findings: A small hole drilled into the sarcophagus found purple linen, blue fabric, grains of red incense and tiny bone fragments, which carbon dating placed in the 1st or 2nd century. The marble slab above, inscribed PAULO APOSTOLO MART, dates to the 4th or 5th century. The results fit the tradition but cannot prove the bones are Paul's.
pages.account_teaching: The Church honors Paul, with Peter, as an apostle whose witness to Christ in Rome ended in martyrdom. Praying at his tomb joins pilgrims to the apostolic faith he handed on.
pages.prep_prayer:
Now to him who by the power at work within us is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus to all generations, for ever and ever. Amen.

St. Paul, Ephesians 3:20–21.
pages.prep_readings:
• Acts 9:1–19: Saul meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus.
  • Acts 28:14–16, 30–31: Paul reaches Rome and preaches there openly.
  • Romans 1:1–17: Paul's greeting to the Christians of Rome.
  • Philippians 1:20–26: "To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."
  • 2 Timothy 4:6–8: "I have fought the good fight."
